                           PIPER RANDOLPH'S INITIAL BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
I. INTRODUCTION
Intervenor Piper Randolph respectfully submits this Initial Brief as the granddaughter of Nelda
Howton and the daughter of Stacy Randolph. Ms. Randolph has a direct family interest in the
Howton property because it is the land her family has used, maintained, and expects to pass to
the next generation. She opposes approval of Route 894 and any other route that uses Link F-20.
This brief addresses the impact of Link F-20 from the perspective of a younger family member
who stands to inherit the place in the future. The proposed 765-kV transmission line would not
merely affect a present landowner for a short period of time. It would place a permanent
industrial burden on a family home, working agricultural property, and rural community that Ms.
Randolph and future generations would be left to live with, maintain, and protect.
Ms. Randolph requests that the Administrative Law Judges recommend rejection of any route
using Link F-20 and instead recommend Preferred Route 296, or another route that avoids Link
F-20 and better protects residences, agricultural operations, community values, historical and
aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the long-term use of family land.
II. FAMILY AND FUTURE-OWNERSHIP INTEREST
Piper Randolph's interest is different from that of her mother, Stacy Randolph, and her
grandmother, Nelda Howton. Her concern is not limited to the immediate disruption caused by
construction. Her concern is the long-term impact of a 765-kV line on property that is intended
to remain in the family and be inherited by the next generation.
The Howton property is not unused land waiting for a utility corridor. It is a family residence and
rural property used for cattle, horses, poultry, gardening, hunting, outdoor family activities, and
ordinary agricultural operations. The route decision will determine whether the next generation
inherits a usable rural homestead or inhe]its a property permanently burdened by a major
transmission facility.
That future impact matters under the Commission's routing criteria. Community values,
historical and aesthetic values, and environmental integrity are not limited to present-day


                                                  1
 inconvenience. They include whether a route protects the continued character, usefulness, and
family legacy of the land.
III. APPLICABLE LEGAL STANDARD
Under PURA Section 37.056(c), the Commission must consider factors relevant to the need for
the project and the proper routing of the proposed transmission line. PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)
specifically requires consideration of community values, recreational and park areas, historical
and aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.
Those factors should be applied to the actual facts shown by affected families and local
wimesses. A route may look acceptable on a map but still be unreasonable when it places
concentrated burdens on homes, agricultural improvements, churches, cultural resources, storm-
recovery areas, and family land intended to remain in use for future generations.
IV. ARG·UMENT
A. Link F-20 would place a permanent burden on family land intended for future
generations.
The proposed line would be placed close to the Howton residence and agricultural
improvements. That proximity would affect not only Nelda Howton's current use of the property,
but also Piper Randolph's future interest in inheriting and preserving the place.
A 765-kV transmission line is not a temporary inconvenience. It would change the visual
character, usable space, quiet enjoyment, and long-term value of the property. The ALJs should
consider that Link F-20 would shift a permanent infrastructure burden onto a family homestead
rather than selecting an available route that avoids those concentrated impacts.
B. The Howton property remains an active rural homestead, not vacant land.
The evidence shows that the property supports a home, barns, fencing, corrals, livestock uses,
cattle production, horses, poultry, gardening, hunting, and outdoor family use. Those uses give
the property its rural character and explain why Link F-20 would be especially harmful.
A route that cuts through or near active family agricultural land can affect access, fencing,
livestock management, property maintenance, outdoor use, and the ability of future family
members to continue using the property as it has historically been used.
C. Community values weigh against Link F-20.
The Cedar Valley and Salado-area community is made up of homes, farms, churches, families,
and rural neighbors who rely on the land and each other. Community values include the way this
area functions as a rural community, not just the number of structures counted on a route map.
Cedar Valley Church is part of that community life. It serves as a place of worship, gathering,
community support, and recovery. Placing a major 765-kV transmission line on Link F-20 would
add an industrial feature near a community institution and would further burden an area that has
already faced severe storm damage.




                                                 2
 D. Buttermilk Creek and the Gault-area cultura~ concerns support avoiding Link F-20.
Ms. Randolph also asks the ALJs to give weight to the cultural and historical concerns associated
with Buttermilk Creek and the Gault archeological area. These features are part of the broader
cultural landscape of the Cedar Valley area.
When a route raises concerns near a culturally significant creek and archeological area, those
concerns should be weighed carefully under historical and aesthetic values and environmental
integrity. A route that avoids or reduces those concerns should be preferred over Link F-20.

E. Tornado recovery and emergency conditions make additional infrastructure burdens
unreasonable.
The Cedar Valley area has already experienced significant tornado damage and continuing
recovery concerns. Adding a 765-kV transmission line in or near the same affected community
would increase the practical and emotional burden on families still dealing with storm
vulnerability and recovery.
The evidence also raises concerns about wildfire risk, vegetation, emergency access, and rural
response conditions. These are localized facts that should be given meaningful weight when
comparing Link F-20 to alternatives.
F. Existing power-line infrastructure should not be used to justify piling another burden
onto the same families.
Ms. Randolph recognizes that routing criteria may consider existing compatible rights-of-way.
However, the existence of the Bartlett power line on or near Link F-20 should not automatically
justify adding another major transmission facility in the same affected area.
The better question is whether the cumulative impact is fair and reasonable after considering
residences, livestock operations, community resources, safety, environmental integrity, and long-
term family use of the land. One existing line should not mean that the same families and the
same rural community must bear every additional infrastructure burden.
G. Preferred Route 296, or another non-F-20 route, better protects the routing values at
issue.
Ms. Randolph requests that the ALJs recommend Preferred Route 296 or another route that
avoids Link F-20. The local evidence shows that Link F-20 would impose concentrated and
avoidable impacts on a family homestead, agricultural land, church and community resources,
cultural-resource concerns, storm-recovery areas, wildfire-prone vegetation, and future
inheritance interests.
If the ALJs evaluate Link F-20 against Link F-21, Ms. Randolph requests that the ALJs give
meaningful weight to the local evidence showing that F-21 would avoid or reduce the most
serious harms associated with F-20. The route ultimately recommended should minimize harm to
existing homes, future family ownership, agricultural operations, cultural resources, and the
established rural community.
V. PROPOSED FINDINGS SUPPORTED BY PIPER RANDOLPH'S POSITION
1. Piper Randolph is the granddaughter of Nelda Howton and the daughter of Stacy Randolph.




                                                3
 2. Ms. Randolph has a direct future interest in the Howton property because she is expected to
   inherit the place in the future.
3. Ms. Randolph opposes Route 894 and any other route that uses Link F-20.
4. The Howton property is a family homestead and working rural property used for agricultural,
   livestock, outdoor, and family purposes.
5. Link F-20 would impose long-term impacts on the property that would affect both current
   and future family use.
6. Community values in the Cedar Valley area include homes, farms, churches, rural neighbors,
   storm recovery, and the continued family use of land.
7. Cedar Valley Church is a community and cultural gathering place that should be considered
   when evaluating Link F-20.
8. Buttermilk Creek and the Gault-area cultural concerns support careful scrutiny of routes that
   create avoidable impacts in that area.
9. The existing Bartlett power line should not automatically justify adding another major
   transmission facility on or near Link F-20 without careful review of cumulative impacts.
10. The routing factors in PURA Section 37.056(c)(4) support giving weight to Ms. Randolph's
    concerns regarding community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental
    integrity, and future use of family land.
11. Preferred Route 296, or another route that avoids Link F-20, would better protect the interests
    identified by Ms. Randolph.

VI. PRAYER
For these reasons, Intervenor Piper Randolph respectfully requests that the Administrative Law
Judges recommend that the Commission reject Route 894 and any other route utilizing Link
F-20.
Ms. Randolph further requests that the Administrative Law Judges recommend approval of
Preferred Route 296, or another route that avoids Link F-20 and better protects residences,
agricultural operations, community values, church and cultural resources, storm recovery,
wildfire safety, aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the future inheritance and use of
family land.
Ms. Randolph requests all other relief to which she may be justly entitled.
